description.summary: The jackalope is a mythical North American hare with antelope or deer antlers, originating as a 1930s taxidermy creation by the Herrick brothers in Douglas, Wyoming. It is the most famous American example of an old global folkloric tradition of horned hares.
description.full: The jackalope is a mythical creature of American folklore, depicted as a jackrabbit with the antlers of a pronghorn antelope or deer. The modern phenomenon traces to Douglas, Wyoming in the early 1930s, where brothers Douglas Herrick (1920–2003) and Ralph Herrick are credited with mounting a jackrabbit head to a set of deer antlers and selling the first specimen to Roy Ball of the La Bonte Hotel for ten dollars in 1932. The fabrication tapped a much older tradition: medieval and early-modern European naturalists illustrated the 'lepus cornutus' or horned hare in bestiaries and natural-history compendia, the Bavarian wolpertinger remains a related taxidermy tradition, and the Persian / Arabic al-mi'raj is a horned hare of medieval Islamic mythography. The Wyoming variant rapidly became roadside-attraction kitsch and a regional tall-tale staple, complete with claims of human-voice mimicry, lightning-fast running, attack behavior, and 'jackalope milk' with medicinal properties. A widely-cited biological cause for at least some original sightings is infection by the Shope papillomavirus (named for Richard E. Shope), which causes large keratinous, horn-shaped tumors to grow on the heads of cottontails and jackrabbits. Douglas, Wyoming has self-styled the 'Jackalope Capital of the World' since 1965, with a city statue, a 'jackalope hunting license' sold by the chamber of commerce, and repeated state-legislature attempts (2005, 2013, 2015) to designate the jackalope Wyoming's official mythological creature.

etymology.origin: Portmanteau of 'jackrabbit' and 'antelope'; coined in the United States, popularized by the Herrick brothers' Douglas, Wyoming taxidermy work in the 1930s

related_phenomena.name: Wolpertinger
related_phenomena.description: Bavarian chimeric taxidermy creature with hare body, antlers, fangs, and wings

related_phenomena.name: Al-mi'raj
related_phenomena.description: Single-horned hare from medieval Arabic / Persian mythography

related_phenomena.name: Lepus cornutus
related_phenomena.description: Pre-modern European 'horned hare' described in early natural-history texts

related_phenomena.name: Skvader
related_phenomena.description: Swedish taxidermy chimera (hare with grouse wings) created 1918

features.description: Pronghorn-antelope or deer-style antlers grafted onto the head; in the Herrick original, deer antlers
Body and head of a black-tailed jackrabbit (Lepus californicus) or related hare
Standard lagomorph dentition; in tall-tale lore exaggerated as 'fangs'

physical.morphology: Standard lagomorph (hare) morphology with antlers added by taxidermy. There is no biological basis for antler growth on a leporid; the closest natural analogue is keratinous papillomas caused by Shope papillomavirus, which are horn-like but not true antlers.

abilities.description: In tall tales, jackalopes are said to mimic human voices, often singing along with cowboy campfire songs
Tall tales describe the jackalope as the 'most aggressive of all rabbit species', willing to attack humans with its antlers
Folk claim that female jackalope milk has medicinal value; central to the Douglas, Wyoming tourist mythos

behavior.diet: Tall tales describe a diet including whiskey; in the underlying lagomorph, grasses and forbs
patterns: Most often 'sighted' on roadside curio-shop walls
Tall-tale stories cluster around cowboy campfires
Modern reports concentrated around Douglas, Wyoming tourism

range.description: Folklore range covers the American West, especially Wyoming, with secondary tall-tale presence across Nebraska, South Dakota, Montana, and Colorado. The wider 'horned hare' tradition is global, with European (wolpertinger, lepus cornutus) and Middle Eastern (al-mi'raj) analogues.

hotspots.name: Douglas, Wyoming
hotspots.notes: Site of the Herrick brothers' original taxidermy and the first jackalope sale to the La Bonte Hotel

first_recorded.source: Herrick family oral history; Wyoming state recognition narratives

peak_activity_periods.description: Roadside-attraction era; postcards, taxidermy mounts, and tall tales spread nationally
Repeated Wyoming legislative attempts to declare the jackalope the state's official mythological creature

temporal.seasonal_patterns: No biological pattern; tourist-driven seasonality peaks in summer in Douglas, Wyoming

origins.cultural_roots: Tall-tale tradition of the American West, fused with a much older transatlantic tradition of horned hares (lepus cornutus) in European natural history and the al-mi'raj of Persian / Arabic mythography.
origins.earliest_accounts: The modern jackalope was created in Douglas, Wyoming by Douglas and Ralph Herrick in the early 1930s; the first taxidermy specimen was sold to Roy Ball of the La Bonte Hotel in 1932.
origins.folklore_connections: Continuous with the European wolpertinger (Bavaria), the Swedish skvader, the al-mi'raj, and the lepus cornutus illustrated in 16th–18th century European bestiaries.

timeline.event: Douglas and Ralph Herrick of Douglas, Wyoming sell their first taxidermy jackalope to Roy Ball at the La Bonte Hotel for $10
timeline.significance: Creation of the modern American jackalope
timeline.source: Herrick family oral history; Smithsonian Magazine

timeline.event: Richard E. Shope, M.D., describes the cottontail rabbit papillomavirus that causes horn-like tumors on rabbits
timeline.significance: Provides a plausible biological substrate for older horned-hare folklore
timeline.source: Shope, R. E. (1933), Journal of Experimental Medicine

timeline.event: Douglas, Wyoming officially declares itself the 'Jackalope Capital of the World'
Death of Douglas Herrick, co-creator of the jackalope, age 82
timeline.significance: Obituary coverage in The New York Times and elsewhere reaffirmed the Herrick origin story

timeline.event: First Wyoming state legislative attempt to designate the jackalope the official mythological creature of Wyoming

history.modern_era: The jackalope remains a heavily commercialized icon of the American West: roadside taxidermy, tourism, novelty 'jackalope hunting licenses' issued by the Douglas chamber of commerce, references in films (Pixar's 'Boundin'', 2003), video games (Red Dead Redemption series), and continued legislative interest in Wyoming.

physical.name: Herrick brothers' first jackalope
physical.description: Original taxidermy mount of a jackrabbit head with deer antlers, created by Douglas and Ralph Herrick and sold to Roy Ball at the La Bonte Hotel, Douglas, Wyoming.
physical.analysis: Acknowledged hoax / craft object, not a biological specimen.
physical.source: Herrick family oral history; Smithsonian Magazine

trace.name: Shope papillomavirus tumors in wild lagomorphs
trace.description: Cottontail rabbit papillomavirus (Shope papillomavirus) causes large keratinous, horn-like tumors on the heads and bodies of infected rabbits in the wild.
trace.analysis: Provides a plausible biological substrate for pre-modern horned-hare folklore; widely cited as a likely root of 'lepus cornutus' reports.
trace.source: Shope, R. E. (1933), J. Exp. Med.

scientific.name: Shope papillomavirus origin
scientific.description: Pre-modern reports of horned hares are best explained by wild lagomorphs infected with cottontail rabbit papillomavirus, which produces large, horn-shaped keratinous tumors.
evidence_cited: Shope (1933) Journal of Experimental Medicine description of the virus
Photographic documentation of wild infected rabbits with horn-like growths

skeptical.name: Acknowledged taxidermy hoax
skeptical.description: The modern jackalope is a known craft fabrication originating with the Herrick brothers in Douglas, Wyoming in 1932, propagated by tourism, postcards, and tall-tale tradition.
evidence_cited: Continuous documented production of taxidermy jackalopes since the 1930s
No specimen ever submitted for biological verification

stories: Tall tales of jackalopes mimicking human voices around cowboy campfires
Douglas, Wyoming 'jackalope hunting license' (issued only on June 31, between midnight and 2 AM, to applicants of low IQ)
folklore.beliefs: Universally acknowledged as folklore / hoax in modern usage; embraced as regional identity rather than as a literal cryptid.

literature: Mythical Creatures Bible — Brenda Rosen (jackalope entry)
other: 'Jackalope hunting licenses' sold by the Douglas Chamber of Commerce

researchers.name: Richard E. Shope
researchers.contribution: Identified the cottontail rabbit papillomavirus (Shope papillomavirus) responsible for horn-like growths on wild rabbits, providing a likely substrate for horned-hare folklore

researchers.name: Douglas Herrick
researchers.contribution: Co-creator of the modern Wyoming jackalope as a taxidermy form (1932)

organizations.name: Douglas Chamber of Commerce
organizations.focus: Civic promotion of the jackalope as Douglas, Wyoming's mascot

research.ongoing_studies: Ongoing veterinary and virological study of cottontail rabbit papillomavirus continues; the jackalope itself is studied as folklore and Americana, not biology.

sources.title: Douglas Herrick, 82, Dies; Father of Jackalope
